title: System Implementation

sentences.text: Hello and welcome to the NPTEL MOOCs course on Foundations for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems.
We are going to continue our discussion on system implementation.
So, previously we talked about the importance of the prototype design prototype evaluate cycle.
We learned about different prototyping approaches.
Just to recollect, we have two categories of prototypes: vertical and horizontal.
We have four approaches to build prototypes: low fidelity, medium fidelity, high fidelity, as well as Wizard of Oz.
And we have three ways to use the prototypes: that is thrown away, incremental, and evolutionary usage.
Also, we talked about the expert evaluation techniques.
We talked about two such techniques: cognitive walkthrough and heuristic evaluation, which are used to quickly evaluate the prototypes.

We are going to continue our discussion on another quick evaluation technique, our discussion on evaluation techniques, and we are going to cover another quick evaluation technique: that is the user evaluation.
Along with that, we are also going to briefly talk about how we implemented the modular tour.
So let us talk about The third quick evaluation technique is user evaluation.
Now the basic idea here is, as we have already noted earlier, to get quick feedback from users by asking them questions directly.
So, in this case of user evaluation, we have to involve the users. In the previous two expert evaluation techniques, involvement of users was optional.
But in the case of user evaluation, it is mandatory.
Now, this is often called evaluation with self-reports.
The user feedback is collected with some rating scales, and the data collected is sometimes called subjective or preference data.
Collection of feedback with rating scales is easy compared to more rigorous evaluation techniques.
However, there are two major points of concern.
The first issue is that when we collect user feedback on a rating scale, we collect ratings on items.
Now, these items are essentially questions or statements.
For example, rate the statement 'The controls are easily accessible' on a three-point Likert scale.
Now, the Likert scale is, of course, a well-known rating scale.
And these types of questions or statements will be provided to the users for them to rate on such a scale.
Now, the prerequisite is we have to identify suitable items or questionnaire.
So these items are commonly referred to as questionnaires, although they need not contain questions; they can be statements as well.
Now, it is of course quite challenging to identify suitable questionnaires; that is the first issue.
The second issue is we have two points for data collection.
After every task, so we are assuming that the users are given some tasks, to perform on the prototype, and then we are collecting feedback.
Now, there can be two data collection points.
One is after every task is performed, and the second is at the end of the session where all the tasks are performed.
So, when should we collect the data?
Of course, it is desirable to collect data at both points if feasible.
Otherwise, we have to choose either of these two points.
Now, depending on when we are collecting the data, we have to create suitable questionnaires.
So, corresponding questionnaires may not be the same.
So, questionnaires required to collect data after every task need not be the same as the questionnaires required to collect data after the whole session.
So, depending on these different requirements, we can have different questionnaires.
Already, there are well-known questionnaires.
available which can be directly used.
So, for post-task data collection we have post-task questionnaire such as After Scenario Questionnaire or ASQ designed way back in 1991 by Lewis.
Then Expectation Measure or EM questionnaire designed in 2003 by Albert and Dixon.
Similarly, for post-session data collection, we have post-session questionnaires such as System Usability Scale or SUS, a very popular questionnaire designed in 1996 by Brooke.
Then Computer System Usability Questionnaire CSUQ, again designed by Lewis in 1995.
Questionnaire for User Interface Satisfaction QUIS, designed by Chin et al., in 1988 that is even before then Usefulness Satisfaction and Ease of Use questionnaire or USE proposed by Lund in 2001.
So, as you can see there are different questionnaire sets meant for collecting data at different points of time.
So, let us quickly go through an example from each of these two types of questionnaires to get some idea on the nature of the questionnaires.
So, let us talk about post-task questionnaire we have seen two out of which let us talk about the ASQ After Scenario Questionnaire.
So, it is a post-task questionnaire consists of three statements although we are calling it questionnaire, but essentially there are three statements in that questionnaire.
Users are asked to provide rating on a seven-point rating scale.
for each statement in the questionnaire.
What are those statements?
We will see soon.
Now, ratings range from strongly disagree with the statement, which is rating 1, to strongly agree, which is rating 7.
So, let us see the statements in the questionnaire.
First one is: I am satisfied with the ease of completing the tasks in this scenario.
The user has to rate between 1 to 7.
Two is: I am satisfied with the amount of time it took to complete the tasks in this scenario.
Again, between 1 to 7, the user has to rate the satisfaction level.
Third is: I am satisfied with the support information that is comprised of online help, messages, documentation when completing the tasks.
User has to rate this statement on a scale of 1 to 7.
So, these three are the statements that comprise the ASQ questionnaire.
Now, the first statement is related to the effectiveness measure of usability.
Efficiency aspect is covered in the second statement, and all three taken together represent satisfaction.
We can roughly map the three measures of usability as mentioned in the ISO definition to these three statements.
How are we going to use the feedback?
We can consider the average rating for each statement collected from all the users who participated in the evaluation or the average rating for all statements taken together.
So, either we can average out For each statement or for all statements taken together, we can take an average value.
So either way is possible.
Now let us talk about another questionnaire that is SUS, the System Usability Scale.
So this is a post-session questionnaire.
Earlier we talked about a post-task questionnaire.
Now this is a post-session questionnaire.
That means it is administered or the feedback is collected at the end of the session when users completed all the tasks.
Now it consists of 10 statements.
Again we are calling it a questionnaire but it contains statements rather than questions.
Out of these 10, half or 5 statements are positively worded.
These are statement numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9.
Assuming that we have Number the statements from 1 to 10.
So, every alternative statement starting from the first one is positively worded and the other half is negatively worded, that is 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10.
Let us have a look at the statements.
Now, question number 1 or statement number 1, you can see is: I think that I would like to use this system frequently.
So, this is a positively worded statement.
2 is: I found the system unnecessarily complex.
This is a negatively worded statement.
Statement number 3 is: I thought the system was easy to use.
Again, positively worded.
4 is: I think I would need the support of a technical person to be able to use the system, negatively worded.
So, as you can see, first and second statements are related.
One is positively worded, the other one is the negatively worded version of the same statement.
Similarly, 3 and 4 are related.
5 and 6 are also related.
5 is: I found the various functions in this system were well integrated, whereas 6 says: I thought the system was too inconsistent.
So, 6 is the negative version of 5.
Similarly, 8 is the negative version of 7.
7 states that I would imagine that most people would learn to use the system very quickly, whereas 8 says that I found the system very cumbersome to use.
Finally, 10 is the negative version of 9.
9 says I felt very confident using the system, whereas 10 says I needed to learn a lot of things before I could get going with this system.
Now, each of these statements a user is supposed to rate on a scale of 1 to 5.
That is a 5-point agreement scale where 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree.
In the ASQ questionnaire, the rating scale was 1 to 7.
Here it is 1 to 5.
Now, how to use the rating?
Earlier we saw that we can use the rating for ASQ, that is, the post-task questionnaire, by just taking the average either question-wise or with all three statements taken together.
Here it is a little bit different.

Here, what we can do is we can combine the ratings for all 10 statements to obtain an overall SUS score using the formula S, that is the score, equals the summation of ri minus 1 plus the summation of 5 minus ri; this whole thing is multiplied by 2.5, where ri is the rating for the ith statement, and i ranges from 1 to 10.

So, when i is taking the values of the positive statements, that is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, the expression is ri minus 1, so rating minus 1, and when it is the negative statements, That is 2, 4, 6, 8, 9. Then we use the expression 5 minus R i. Then we add these two weighted sums, add these two sums, and then multiply it with 2.5.
That is the formulation to combine the scores.
We can interpret the score as a percentage.
So, whatever result we get after doing this calculation, we can convert it to a percentage directly.
Typically, a SUS score around 70 percent or higher is desirable.
So, we can assume that if the score is 70 percent or higher, then the interface is usable.
If it is below 70 percent, scores lower than that 70 percent might indicate usability problems.
So, we may need to have a re-look at the design.
Unlike the expert evaluation technique, as you can see here, the scores do not give a detailed report because it is coming from the users.
Users themselves may not know the reason for their satisfaction or dissatisfaction.
So, in that case, the designers have to further brainstorm and identify the problem.
It will only tell that there is a problem or not.
If the SUS score is greater than 70% or equal to 70%, then there is likely to be no problem or very minimal problem not to be bothered about.
If it is less than 70%, then there are problems, but these problems the designers have to find out through further brainstorming.
Maybe by looking at the scores of the different statements and then inferring from there where exactly the problem is.

So, the previous evaluation techniques probably or most likely are Better for the designers; it gives more detailed reports from each evaluator so that it is easier for the designer to identify the problems.
In this case, it is not so easy.
It can identify the problem quickly by taking user feedback in the form of ratings, but pinpointing the problem requires more effort from the designers.
Now, ASQ, SUS, these are all, Questionnaires that are meant for interactive systems, not specifically meant for extended reality systems.
So they are generic questionnaires applicable to any interactive system.
Now there are few questionnaires which are more commonly used in and specifically designed for XR.
Some of these questionnaires we have already discussed in module 1 where In lecture 11, lecture number 11, we talked about questionnaires specifically meant for cyber sickness.
Let us quickly recap those.
So, we have the simulator sickness questionnaire or SSQ.
This is the most extensively used.
Other relevant questionnaires are the virtual reality sickness questionnaire, VRSQ, and the cyber sickness questionnaire, CSQ.
It is good for evaluating VR experiences with HMDs.
Shorter and more precise, more concise questionnaires are there to assess specific conditions such as misery scale or MIS, fast motion sickness scale or FMS.
We can also measure susceptibility to CS.
Using Motion History Questionnaire, MHQ, Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire, MSSQ, Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire, VIMSSQ.
Also, commonly used questionnaires to assess overall discomfort are also there, such as nausea scale, motion sickness assessment questionnaire or MSAQ and so on.
So, these are specifically designed for immersive experiences.
To be more precise, these are specifically designed for specific aspects of immersive experience that is primarily related to cyber sickness.
Now, let us quickly move our focus to how we implemented these implementation ideas in our case that is Majuli VR Tour.
So, whatever we have learned so far, namely design considerations, prototype building and expert evaluations, are meant to fine tune the design.
The next stage is full scale system implementation.
And that implementation we are going to briefly talk about here in the case of Majuli.
So, the tour was developed using the Unity engine, the XR engine, Unity version 2021.3.22f1.
It was developed for Oculus Quest 2 platform and also Android smartphones.
Where we used older version of Android, Android version 6.
We employed the XR toolkit for the Quest version and the Google VR SDK for the Cardboard version.
Also, we utilized Autodesk Maya software to create 3D models for the immersive experience where we used the real images as references and utilized the real images as textures on modeled objects.
Now, there are some concerns.
One concern was optimizing the size.
So, initial application size because the content was heavy to cover the entire geographic spread, the application size was 9.85 GB.
Now, to reduce the space requirements, we used cloud to store all the videos, cloud services.
When a user clicks on the video thumbnail from the video player in the Quest, that is the video player that is seen on that tablet interface, then the video is loaded from the cloud and played.
So it is not that the video is always there in the client device.
So it led to the reduced application size of 5.1 GB.
Now we also created a mobile version to be experienced with Google Cardboard.
This 5.1 GB size application was not suitable for deployment on mobiles.
So what we used is compressed images.
So whatever images, 360 degree or 2D images we have captured in high resolution, we compressed those.
To reduce the storage requirements, also we reduced the video playback support for many of the cases except one or two video playback supports.
We removed most of the video playback support for making it deployable on mobile devices.
So, with those optimization processing done, the size got reduced to 0.7 GB which we deployed on mobiles to be experienced with a Google Cardboard device.
Just let us have a quick look at the different optimizations we achieved.
So, in the Oculus Quest version, the size was 5.1 GB, whereas for the mobile or cardboard version, it was 0.7 GB.
Number of images in Oculus Quest, all the images, 597.
We also used all the images, but in a compressed form in the cardboard version.
Number of cultural videos published.
It was 11 there, but no such videos were used in the cardboard or mobile version.
Number of drone videos, 8 videos were used in the Quest version, whereas no videos were used in the mobile version.
360 degree videos, there were 5 used in the Quest version and 1 used in the cardboard version for the initial experience.
Development platform used Unity in both cases.
SDKs used XR toolkit for the Oculus Quest and Google VR for the cardboard version.
And the OS requirement was Android 6.0 in both cases.
So let us quickly go through the implementation in the form of demos.
Okay, so let us have a look at the implementation of the Majuli VR tours.
So, we have made three implementations.
Accordingly, let us have a look at each of these three.
So, the first one is a tour using 360-degree images, and it was made for the Oculus Quest platform as we said.
Let us quickly have a look in a brief video on the implementation.

So, as you can see, this is the start screen, and then there is this ray casting-based selection method. On the start screen, initial videos and other things are to be played, videos on Majuli and also a tutorial, and then the user can make selections on the start screen.
It shows information about Majuli and also it talks about how to control the system, how to use the system.
So, different aspects of the Majuli island are shown.
Then there is this user group selection, and that is followed by a boat ride experience, that is, traversing the river through a boat from the mainland to the island.
It is actually a 360-degree video captured during our field trips, and that is used here to give the user the experience of traveling by boat.
Then the user reaches the riverbank, and there, this tablet interface appears.
The user can select a location using the tablet interface, the map, and then can go to a particular location.
There once the user enters a location, then this place appears.
Where using the arrow keys user can move forward, backward and also you can see the icons meant for information.
Plus at a place there is notification if there are some cultural videos to be experienced and that gets played on the tablet interface as we have discussed before.
So user can move from one point to another.
Using the overall island map on the tablet interface and this is the mini map or the wild in miniature support as we have discussed.
So, in a location where the user is Is depicted on a minimap of the location where you can see on this minimap interface, there are white dots.
Each white dot represents a 360 degree image.
So when user moves, that means moving from one image to another and the user's current location is marked in green.
And you can hear the, so there is this, there is this ambient sound also added.
And to travel from one point to another along with teleportation, we have used this vehicle metaphor, which is kind of route planning.
The route is fixed, but user can experience the movement along the road as if the user is sitting on a vehicle and moving along the road.
Once reaching a destination, user can move forward by following the arrow keys as shown here.

And each selection of arrow key actually transports the user from one image, to the next image and during transitions we have used techniques as discussed earlier to enhance the quality of experience.
So, at different points different cultural videos are to be experienced and also different activities can be experienced.
This is the implementation for Oculus Quest using 360-degree images and the cultural videos as well as 360-degree videos.
Our next implementation is the tool using a 3D model.
So, earlier we used 360-degree images and videos to create the experience; here we used 3D models to create the experience.
So, as you can see here, the model of the entrance to a Satra is created and used for the experience, unlike the previous case where we used the actual 360-degree images.
So, this is for Kamalabadi Satra, a prominent spot on the Majuli Island.
Then the entire campus was modeled and then you can move along the roads to enter different parts of the campus.
Then we have created models for the villages, the dwelling units.
So, this is 3D model based.
And to create the models, of course, we have used the texture from the real images and then used those to create a realistic looking model.
Now, this model-based implementation was also meant for headsets, Oculus Quest headset.
The third implementation is for mobile devices.
So, this was one done to experience with a Google Cardboard where you can insert your phone and you can have a 360-degree experience.
So, the deployment would be on your smartphone, and then the smartphone can be inserted into the Google Cardboard device, and then you can experience it.
So, this is the kind of experience.
Here we have not used videos, most of the videos, to optimize the size as mentioned earlier.
Simpler controls were provided, and fewer features were provided.
So, this is the boat ride experience which we kept.
In the same tablet interface, but in a different form, and also a minimap is there as you can see at each place.
However, in most of the places we have not used the cultural videos to save on space.
Some prominent videos were used, but not all.
So, this obviously gives a more reduced form of experience as compared to the full-fledged version implemented for the headsets such as Oculus Quest.
But other modes of navigation, selection, and manipulation were more or less the same.
We have arrows and so on.
Okay, let us summarize the discussion that we have done so far.
So, we talked about the design prototype evaluate lifecycle, how to build and evaluate prototypes.
Also, we talked about the expert evaluation techniques and how we implemented the Majuli VR Tour.
So, with that we have come to the end of the discussion on the implementation part.
The next part that is remaining on this implementation concept, implementation topic is how to evaluate for usability through full-fledged user evaluation.
So, previously we talked about quick and cheap evaluation using expert evaluation techniques or some quick user evaluation techniques.
Next, we are going to talk about empirical evaluation in detail.
So, I hope you could follow the topics and able to understand the concepts.
So, looking forward to meeting you in the next part of the lecture.
Till then, thank you, goodbye and happy learning.

parts.objective: Compare post-task and post-session user evaluation methodologies, such as ASQ and SUS

key_points.text: User evaluation is a technique where feedback is collected from users by asking questions directly, making user involvement mandatory, often resulting in subjective preference data.
Post-task questionnaires, like ASQ, use a seven-point rating scale to assess usability across specific measures such as ease of completing tasks, time taken, and support information.
The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire consisting of 10 statements (5 positive and 5 negative), with scores calculated using a specific weighted summation formula.
For the SUS, a score of 70 percent or higher is typically considered desirable, indicating that the interface is usable.
Unlike expert evaluations, user feedback gathered via ratings does not provide a detailed report on *why* a user is satisfied or dissatisfied, requiring further brainstorming from designers.

terms.name: User evaluation
terms.definition: User evaluation is an evaluation technique used to quickly gather feedback directly from users by asking them questions. Unlike expert evaluation, the involvement of users in user evaluation is mandatory.

terms.name: Evaluation with self-reports
terms.definition: Evaluation with self-reports is a method where user feedback is collected directly from the users, often by asking them questions.

terms.name: Subjective or preference data
terms.definition: Subjective or preference data refers to the user feedback collected during evaluations, typically gathered using rating scales.

terms.name: Rating scale
terms.definition: A rating scale is a tool used to collect user feedback, such as providing users with statements to rate on a defined scale like the Likert scale.

terms.name: Likert scale
terms.definition: The Likert scale is a well-known type of rating scale that is used by providing users with statements to rate.

terms.name: Questionnaire
terms.definition: Questionnaire is an instrument used to collect feedback that can contain either questions or statements for users to rate.

terms.name: Post-session questionnaire
terms.definition: Post-session questionnaire is designed to collect data at the end of a user evaluation session after all tasks have been completed.

terms.name: Post-task questionnaire
terms.definition: Post-task questionnaire is used to collect data immediately after a task is performed, and these questions need not be the same as those used after the entire session.

terms.name: After Scenario Questionnaire
terms.definition: After Scenario Questionnaire is a specific post-task questionnaire that consists of three statements, which users rate on a seven-point scale.

terms.name: System Usability Scale
terms.definition: System Usability Scale is a well-known post-session questionnaire used for collecting data on the usability of a system.

terms.name: ASQ questionnaire
terms.definition: The ASQ questionnaire is a usability evaluation tool consisting of three statements. These statements collectively represent user satisfaction by covering three aspects of usability: effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.

terms.name: Effectiveness measure
terms.definition: Effectiveness measure is one of the three measures of usability that can be roughly mapped to the first statement of the ASQ questionnaire.

terms.name: Efficiency aspect
terms.definition: Efficiency aspect is one of the three measures of usability that is covered in the second statement of the ASQ questionnaire.

terms.name: System Usability Scale score
terms.definition: The System Usability Scale score is calculated by combining the ratings from all statements using a specific formula that weights positive and negative statements differently. This resulting score can then be converted and interpreted as a percentage.

parts.objective: Identify and describe specific questionnaires used to evaluate comfort and sickness in immersive XR experiences

key_points.text: Generic questionnaires (like ASQ and SUS) are applicable to any interactive system, not specifically extended reality (XR).
The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is the most extensively used questionnaire for XR.
The cyber sickness questionnaire (CSQ) is used for evaluating VR experiences with Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs). (cited sentences)

The misery scale (MIS) and fast motion sickness scale (FMS) are shorter and more precise questionnaires for assessing specific conditions, while the Motion History Questionnaire (MHQ) and Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MSSQ) are used to measure susceptibility to cyber sickness. (cited sentences)

terms.name: Simulator Sickness Questionnaire
terms.definition: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire is the most extensively used questionnaire specifically designed for evaluating simulator sickness.

terms.name: Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire
terms.definition: The Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire is a relevant questionnaire used for evaluating VR experiences.

terms.name: Cyber Sickness Questionnaire
terms.definition: The Cyber Sickness Questionnaire is a relevant questionnaire used for evaluating experiences related to cyber sickness.

terms.name: Misery Scale
terms.definition: The Misery Scale is a shorter and more precise questionnaire used to assess specific conditions.

terms.name: Fast Motion Sickness Scale
terms.definition: The Fast Motion Sickness Scale is a shorter and more precise questionnaire designed to assess specific conditions.

terms.name: Motion History Questionnaire
terms.definition: The Motion History Questionnaire is a specific questionnaire used to measure susceptibility to cyber sickness (CS).

terms.name: Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire
terms.definition: The Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire is a specific questionnaire used to measure susceptibility to cyber sickness (CS).

terms.surface: Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire
terms.name: Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire
terms.definition: The Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire is a specific questionnaire used to measure susceptibility to cyber sickness (CS).

terms.name: Nausea Scale
terms.definition: The Nausea Scale is one of the commonly used questionnaires designed to assess overall discomfort during immersive experiences.

terms.name: Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire
terms.definition: The Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire is a commonly used questionnaire designed to assess overall discomfort in immersive experiences.

parts.objective: Compare implementation methods, technologies, and optimization strategies used to deploy VR experiences on different platforms

key_points.text: The VR tour was developed using the Unity XR engine (2021.3.22f1) for both Oculus Quest and Android.
The application size was optimized from 9.85 GB (initial) to 5.1 GB (Quest) by utilizing cloud storage for videos.
The mobile version (Google Cardboard) was reduced to 0.7 GB using compressed images and limiting video playback support.
Different SDKs were used for the platforms: XR toolkit for Oculus Quest and Google VR SDK for Cardboard.

terms.name: Full scale system implementation
terms.definition: This stage represents the complete execution of the system after the initial design and prototyping phases have been completed and fine-tuned.

terms.name: Unity engine
terms.definition: Unity is the engine used for developing the virtual tour, serving as the core software platform for the immersive experience.

terms.name: XR engine
terms.definition: XR engine is the engine utilized for developing the virtual tour.

terms.name: Oculus Quest 2 platform
terms.definition: Oculus Quest 2 platform is one of the target devices for the virtual tour, requiring the use of the XR toolkit for implementation.

terms.name: XR toolkit
terms.definition: XR toolkit is the specific set of development tools employed to build the application for the Quest version.

terms.name: Google VR SDK
terms.definition: Google VR SDK is the specific toolkit utilized when developing the mobile version of the experience for the Cardboard device.

terms.name: Autodesk Maya software
terms.definition: Autodesk Maya software is the program utilized to create the three-dimensional models used within the immersive virtual experience.

terms.name: Cloud
terms.definition: Cloud is a storage solution where large video files are kept external to the device and are loaded dynamically when a user requests them.

terms.name: Google Cardboard device
terms.definition: The Google Cardboard device is the mobile platform used for experiencing the virtual tour, which requires specialized optimization strategies to function correctly.

parts.objective: Compare three distinct implementations of a VR tour using 360-degree images, 3D models, and mobile devices

key_points.text: The first implementation used 360-degree images for Oculus Quest, incorporating features like ray casting, a tablet interface, a minimap showing 360-degree images, and a vehicle metaphor for route planning. (S177-S200)

The second implementation utilized 3D models, created using real-world textures, to render locations like the Satra campus, offering an experience different from that using 360-degree images. (S201-S209)
The third implementation for mobile devices (Google Cardboard) was optimized for size, resulting in simpler controls and fewer cultural videos compared to the headset versions. (S210-S220)

terms.name: 360-degree image
terms.definition: These are panoramic images that allow the user to view a full 360-degree environment, often used in VR tours.

terms.name: Ray casting-based selection method
terms.definition: This method is used on the start screen to allow the user to make selections within the virtual environment.

terms.name: Tablet interface
terms.definition: This is an interface displayed to the user that allows selection of locations using a map and displays information or cultural videos.

terms.surface: mini map or the wild in miniature support
terms.name: Mini map
terms.definition: This is a support system within the interface that shows the overall island map, depicting the user's location and points of interest as white dots.

terms.name: Vehicle metaphor
terms.definition: This is a method used for travel between points where the route is fixed, allowing the user to experience movement as if they were sitting on a vehicle.

terms.name: 3D model
terms.definition: This refers to a digital representation of real-world objects or locations, such as a campus or village, used to create the virtual experience.

terms.name: Texture
terms.definition: Texture is used from real images and applied to 3D models to make the virtual objects and environments look realistic.

terms.name: Oculus Quest headset
terms.definition: This is a specific headset device designed for implementation purposes, such as experiencing a VR tour.

terms.name: Mobile device
terms.definition: Mobile devices serve as one platform for implementation, allowing users to experience the VR tour via their smartphone.

terms.name: Google Cardboard
terms.definition: This is a device used for mobile VR experiences where a smartphone is inserted into it to provide a 360-degree viewing experience.

terms.name: Expert evaluation technique
terms.definition: These are evaluation techniques used to test and implement projects, such as the Majuli VR Tour, which is described as a quick and cheap form of evaluation.

terms.name: Full fledged user evaluation
terms.definition: This is a comprehensive method of user evaluation that comes after quick expert evaluation and is required for the complete implementation concept.

terms.name: Empirical evaluation
terms.definition: This is a type of evaluation that will be discussed in detail, contrasting with quick and cheap expert evaluations.

objectives.text: you'll be able to compare post-task and post-session user evaluation methodologies (such as ASQ and SUS) and identify specific questionnaires used to evaluate comfort and sickness in immersive XR experiences

you'll be able to compare implementation methods, technologies, and optimization strategies used to deploy VR experiences on different platforms, utilizing case studies like distinct VR tours based on 360-degree images and 3D models

lecture_goal: Master the processes of deploying, optimizing, and evaluating immersive virtual reality experiences.
